content: The studies that were excluded from this evidence summary addressed different questions, specifically the use of external compression or surgical methods to treat primary postpartum hemorrhage (PPH). The trials included in the review were published between 2007 and 2018, with the earliest participant enrollment beginning in 2003. One trial compared the use of two types of uterine balloon tamponade devices following vaginal birth: the Bakri balloon (saline-filled) and a condom-loaded Foley catheter (saline-filled). This trial, conducted in a single district hospital in Egypt, involved 66 women who experienced PPH due to uterine atony after vaginal delivery. Participants were randomized to receive either the Bakri balloon or the condom-loaded Foley catheter if their PPH was unresponsive to initial treatments. The first-line treatment consisted of uterine massage and 40 IU of oxytocin, while the second-line treatment involved 1000 µg of rectal misoprostol. Both devices were inflated using the same protocol, starting with 150 mL of saline and increasing up to 400–500 mL. The intervention was deemed unsuccessful if bleeding did not stop within 15 minutes. Vaginal packing with 20 cm of gauze was used in both groups to prevent balloon expulsion. All participants received intravenous cephradine (1 g every 12 hours) following balloon insertion. However, the study did not define PPH or use an accurate method to assess blood loss. Women with traumatic PPH, placental abruption, placenta previa, pregnancy complications (e.g., pre-eclampsia, diabetes, anemia, rheumatic heart disease), or known coagulation disorders were excluded. Additionally, traumatic lesions and retained placental fragments were ruled out under general anesthesia before recruitment. Another trial included in the Cochrane review focused on women with primary PPH during cesarean section. This study, conducted in a military hospital in Saudi Arabia, involved 50 women at ≥28 weeks’ gestation who experienced uncontrolled atonic PPH during cesarean delivery that was unresponsive to standard treatments (not described). Participants were treated with either a Bakri balloon (saline-filled) alone or a Bakri balloon with an additional traction stitch. The balloon was placed intraoperatively within the uterine cavity and inflated with saline after suturing the uterine incision, ensuring it conformed to the uterine contour. No vaginal packing was used in either group. Women in the intervention group received a traction stitch to secure the tamponade. Both groups were administered intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics (unspecified drug and dose) for the first 48 hours postoperatively and oxytocin infusion for the first eight hours. The study did not describe the method of blood loss assessment or define PPH. Women with bleeding due to trauma or placenta previa, as well as those with coagulopathy, were excluded. The study was terminated after 50 cases due to a high rate of balloon displacement in the control group. The Cochrane review reported on the comparison of the Bakri balloon and the condom-loaded Foley catheter for vaginal births. The trial suggested little to no difference between the two devices in reducing the need for blood transfusion (red cells or whole blood). Priority outcomes such as surgical interventions (e.g., hysterectomy, B-Lynch suture), procedure-related complications (e.g., uterine perforation), infections (e.g., endometritis), severe morbidity (e.g., disseminated intravascular coagulation), maternal transfer to intensive care, and maternal fever (≥38°C within the first 24 hours postpartum) were reported, but the evidence was of very low certainty and inconclusive. No other priority outcomes were reported. For cesarean sections, the comparison of the Bakri balloon with and without a traction stitch was reported in one study. However, data were only available for three priority outcomes. The evidence on surgical interventions (e.g., hysterectomy, uterine artery ligation, internal iliac artery ligation, or arterial embolization) was of very low certainty. No other WHO priority outcomes were reported. Additional systematic reviews were considered. The 2012 WHO recommendation was based on observational evidence, as no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were available at the time. A 2019 systematic review included seven RCTs, 15 non-randomized studies, and 69 case series, reporting on the efficacy, effectiveness, and safety of uterine balloon tamponade devices for PPH due to various causes after vaginal and/or cesarean births. The primary outcome was the success of uterine balloon tamponade, defined as cessation of bleeding without maternal death or additional surgical/radiological interventions. Another systematic review focused on uterine balloon tamponade studies in women with refractory PPH presumed to be caused by uterine atony after vaginal birth. This review included five studies published between 2007 and 2019, with two main outcomes: the need for surgical interventions or maternal death, and hysterectomy. Both reviews included one RCT comparing the Bakri balloon with the condom-loaded Foley catheter, already described in the Cochrane review. Improvised uterine balloon tamponade devices may be less effective than purpose-designed devices due to challenges with assembly and insertion. The trial comparing the condom-loaded catheter and the Bakri balloon reported a time to bleeding cessation of 9 minutes (SD 6) for the Bakri balloon and 12 minutes (SD 7) for the condom catheter. Regarding resource requirements, the Cochrane review did not predefine cost or economic outcomes. A systematic review of cost-effectiveness studies identified two high-quality studies using a model-based approach to estimate the incremental costs of introducing uterine balloon tamponade for PPH treatment. Neither study compared the cost-effectiveness of different devices. Both studies relied on published effect estimates from case series rather than meta-analyses or trials. The main resource requirements for uterine balloon tamponade include trained maternity staff, adequate health facilities, and necessary supplies (e.g., Foley catheters, condoms, saline, syringes, and sterile gloves). Placement typically requires IV fluids, instruments (e.g., speculum, forceps), analgesia or anesthesia, and antibiotics. In high-income countries, uterine balloon tamponade is often placed in a surgical theater after uterine cavity exploration to exclude trauma as the cause of bleeding. In lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), placement is commonly performed in the delivery room without uterine cavity exploration. The time to bleeding cessation was reported as 9 minutes (SD 6) for the Bakri balloon and 12 minutes (SD 7) for the condom catheter in a trial comparing the two devices. Supervision and monitoring are essential to ensure appropriate use, stock availability, and quality. Equity considerations suggest that commercially available devices, if effective and safe, may be limited in LMICs due to cost, potentially reducing equity. Conversely, effective and safe improvised devices could increase equity due to their lower cost.
